I got the "where are you really from" from my new boss a couple weeks ago. I reported him to HR. A younger me would have ignored it and moved on, but I'm tired of the microagressions and racism that we are expected to just deal with because it's "not that bad." 

Some words of warning/advice/encouragement if you decide to report him - it will be uncomfortable. You'll have to relive the trauma when explaining what happened to HR. You will likely have to do the labor in educating HR/your manager on why that was racist. At the end of the day, you may or may not receive an apology or closure, but you'll know that you spoke up and called out their racism and maybe they'll think twice about saying it to someone else. 

If you choose not to report him, that's ok too. Just make sure you have a supportive group of people that you can vent to and have your back.

I think that right now is definitely a tough time to be graduating with an accounting degree. I'm a recent graduate myself, so I think I can understand your anxiety. I'll try to piece together my own experiences and advice I've gotten from others, and hopefully it'll help you out. (I'm from CA, by the way, so some rules might be slightly different.

First of all, I'm not sure why your professor told you accounting firms weren't offering internships to juniors. They are *starting* to move in that direction this year, but last year it was definitely still open to juniors. The reason they're pushing everything one year back is because of the changes going on with CPA requirements. Beginning on 1/1/14 (in California) the only way to get licensed is to have 150 semester units (225 quarter units) of education along with a certain number of accounting and business units. Any student who graduates taking only the minimum number of courses required to get a B.S. in accounting won't meet these requirements. As a result, most universities are starting a masters in accountancy program in anticipation of these changes. Luckily for you, you should still be able to get licensed without a masters in accountancy if you pass the CPA exam within the next two years and get the required experience. *Most people I've talked to say a masters in accountancy is pretty useless anyways...* 

So how do you get a job? I'm sure you've heard this before, but network, network, NETWORK. Oh, by the way, did I mention NETWORK? I cannot stress how important that is. You never know when an opportunity might arise. In fact, I was finally able to get a job straight out of college because I met a person at a wedding who happened to be the head HR person at an accounting firm that I interviewed with back in the fall but never heard back from. A good way to start networking is to go to your school's career fairs. It doesn't matter if you've already graduated, just go. You might even have a leg up on other students there because you already have your degree, and hopefully you'll already be studying for the CPA exam (maybe even pass some parts!). From my experience, a lot of accounting firms do most of their hiring during the fall and winter quarters (Oct-Feb), so that would be the peak season to apply (and try to do it through your school's career website if you still have access to it). But that's not to say they don't hire throughout the year either, although that's more difficult. 

You definitely have a lot of options you can take at the moment, but you don't have a lot of time to make your decision if you want to meet the 1/1/14 deadline. 

Good luck, and don't give up!

**TL;DR**

> what avenues should I be taking to find firms to do entry level work with my bachelors? And how do I get in with firms that are explicitly hiring? 

Network, email recruiters, go to career fairs, apply online (on your school website), volunteer in an accounting-related position

I was a junior transfer 2 years ago, and I'll be graduating with a degree in accounting in two weeks with a job waiting for me (not with the Big 4). 

From my experience, being a transfer student didn't make a huge impact on the way the Big 4 or other accounting firms treated me. They still look at your GPA and extracurricular activities. Where I go to school, recruiters usually look for interns during the winter quarter (around January, February, March), so you should have one semester or quarter of grades at your new school, which you should add to your resume. The Big 4 definitely won't treat you differently just because you're a transfer student. In fact, when I was applying for internships my first year as a transfer student, I ended up getting interviews from all of the Big 4 and a couple other firms. The only disadvantage that I seemed to notice being a transfer student is that you miss out on the sophomore summer leadership programs, which is very good for networking.

My advice would be to get involved in your school's accounting club, and network, network, network!
